DILG DIUPWAS RepublE of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA cor. Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City www.dllg.qov.ph OPINION NO. S. JUN 1 1 2025 ATTY. BENJAMIN E. ARITAO, JR. ATTY. GRACE C. PASTORFIDE benjamin@aritaolaw.com grace@aritaolaw.com Dear Attys. Aritao Jr. and Pastorfide: This has reference to your letter dated 27 August 2024 seeking this Department's legal opinion regarding the alleged inaction of the punong barangay to act as witness of your client regarding a property located within the jurisdiction of the barangay. per the representation, you sent a letter to the barangay requesting for assistance to act as witness in the eviction of the tenant in your client's rental property. You then stated that Punong Barangay refused and such refusal has led to the continuous damage experienced by your client — Intergulf Realty Leasing Corporation. You mentioned in your letter dated 24 April 2024 to the Punong Barangay that the tenant has not been paying their rent since October 2023 which urged you to padlock the rental premises. You then indicated that on March II, 2024, you requested assistance from the barangay to lock the aforementioned premises, but the latter instructed you to first tell them of your plans and refused to assist with the locking. Also, you mentioned that you notified the tenant in writing, and that the barangay officials accompanied your client as their witness. You then stated that on March 19, 2024, your client caused the locking of the rental premises and alleged that their contract stipulation authorizes your client to enter, occupy, padlock and take full physical possession of the premises, and it was done without the presence of the barangay officials. However, PB clarified that the reason for the barangay's inaction was due to the absence of order from the court, and he mentioned that they had endorsed the matter to the Philippine National Police (PNP), but the latter likewise declined due to the absence of a court order. Thus, you are requesting assistance from this Department to commence disciplinary proceedings against the barangay officials for their refusal of a lawful request to witness, and for violation of Section 5, R.A. 6713. Regrettably, this Department only exercises general supervision over the Local Government Units. "Mauna, Mahusay at Maaasahan" Trunkline NO. (02) 8876 3454

We respectfully reiterate that a verified complaint against any elective barangay official "shall be filed before the Sangguniang Panlungsod or Sangguniang Bayan whose decision shall be final and executory," pursuant to Section 61 of the Local Government Code, or to the Office of the Ombudsman pursuant to Section 2, Rule III of the Administrative Order No. 07 Rules of Procedure of the Office of the Ombudsman. Hence, should you find merit in your complaint, you can file your verified complaint before the Sangguniang Panlungsod of Quezon City. Be that as it may, for purposes of academic discussion, we are of the considered view that the actions of the Punong Barangay and barangay officials are correct and justifiable. Please be informed that there is nothing in R.A. 7160 otherwise known as the Local Government Code of the Philippines that requires the Punong Barangay and barangay officials to be witnesses when the landlord locks up the rented premises. As such, the Barangay's role is to primarily facilitate mediation between landlords and tenants of the legal process under the Katarungang Pambarangay Law (Barangay Justice System). They do not have the legal authority to evict a tenant or lock up the premises forcibly. The barangay's role is to help both parties reach an amicable settlement to avoid escalating the matter to the courts. In line with this, we agree with the Supreme Court in the case of Viray V. IACI in saying that: "where a lease provides that if the tenants holds over after the expiration of his term, the landlord may enter and take possession of the premises, using all necessary force to obtain the actual possession thereof, and that such entry should not be regarded as a trespass, be sued for as such, or in any wise be considered unlawful, the landlord may forcibly expel the tenant upon the termination of the tenancy, using no more force than is necessary, and will not be liable to the tenant therefor, such a condition in a lease being valid." However, nothing in the aforementioned jurisprudence mandates or precludes barangay officials from witnessing in the locking or taking over of the landlord's property. Thus, the barangay officials may or may not accede to the requests of the landlords to be witnesses in taking back their property from the tenant, as stated in their lease contract. While not legally required to witness the actual locking of the premises, barangay officials may be called to mediate disputes between landlords and tenants. As a practice, some landlords involve barangay officials in the process to ensure that the situation is documented and to prevent potential allegations of illegal eviction. This is more for transparency and protection rather than a legal obligation. I G.R. NO. 81015, July 4, 1991 Page 2 of 3

The opinion of this Department is based solely on the facts and representations you have narrated in your letter and our appreciation of the same. We hope to have addressed your concern accordingly. Thank you. Very truly yours, BY AUTHORITY OF THE SECRETARY: OMEO P. BENITEZ Assistant Secretary for Legal and Legislative Affairs OASLLNRPBILLLS-LRALLD/lasm Page 3 of 3
